title: Incident Hypothesis to Capacity Remediation Playbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

This playbook maps common incident hypotheses to specific capacity remediation actions, decision gates, evidence required for a post-incident review, and automated / manual runbook steps. It is intended as an SRE-facing operational standard for (1) triage during SLO-impacting incidents, (2) immediate capacity remediation to protect user-facing SLOs and error budgets, and (3) evidence collection so that remediation decisions can be validated in postmortem reviews.

When to use this playbook

- Any incident with active SLO degradation (latency P95/P99 or availability breaches).
- Sustained error budget burn (> 10% within 1 hour or > 30% within 24 hours).
- Reproducible hypothesis that maps to capacity, scheduling, or routing (e.g., model hot-loop, tenant noisy neighbor, autoscaler misconfiguration).

Key principles

1. Fast, reversible actions. Prefer conservative capacity hedges that are reversible (burst pools, admission-control throttles, canary drains).
2. Evidence-first escalation. Collect minimum telemetry to validate hypothesis before destructive actions when possible.
3. Protect the customer-facing path. Prioritize latency/availability SLOs over non-critical background work.
4. Communicate decisions with explicit owner and ETA.

Incident hypothesis matrix (quick reference)

| Hypothesis (what we see) | Primary telemetry to validate | Immediate remediation (1–15 min) | Secondary remediation (15–120 min) | Owner | Rollback criteria |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sudden P99 latency spike on text-generation endpoints | Per-route P50/P95/P99, GPU queue length, KV cache hit rate, model hot-pool counts | Shift traffic to warm pool variant (same model, smaller batch) + enable prefix caching for matching routes | Scale dedicated GPU pool by +20% (provision burst reserve), tune batching window -10ms | model-serving oncall | Latency P99 returns to baseline for 10 min and queue length < 50% |
| Error budget burn due to tenant surge (single tenant) | Token rate per tenant, tenant error rate, throttle events | Apply tenant-level throttling: 95th pct rate cap, soft-queue to best-effort lane | Evict soft-queued requests after 5 min, offer customer-facing credit; open incident with CSM | sres/tenant-ops | Tenant rate below soft cap for 30 min or support-acknowledged mitigation |
| Autoscaler flapping causing oscillation and CPU pressure | Scale events, pod churn, provisioning latency, backlog | Temporarily disable aggressive scale policy; pin stable replica count; mark autoscaler in degraded mode | Adjust HPA thresholds, increase stabilization window to 5 min, test in staging then re-enable | infra-autoscale team | No further flapping for 2 stabilization windows (10 min each) |
| KV cache miss storm after model rollout | KV hit ratio, rollout timeline, traffic fingerprint changes | Rollback to previous model variant (fast rollback) + enable warm prefix replication | Run synthetic canary to validate new variant at low concurrency; reintroduce with throttled rollout | runtime-team | Canary passes synthetic workload and KV hit ratio >= 95% |
| Regional capacity hit during provider interruption | Region P50/P95, cross-region failover metrics, routing policy triggers | Failover routing to secondary region (automated) + scale up cross-region capacity | Open cloud capacity request; increase burst quota; update failover runbook and run DR test next 72h | sres/region-oncall | Regional P99 back to baseline and failover return traffic < 10% after 30 min |

Remediation decision flow (step-by-step)

1) Rapid assessment (0–5 minutes)
   - Confirm SLO indicator that triggered alert. Record P50/P95/P99 and current trend.
   - Formulate a short hypothesis: (a) capacity, (b) routing, (c) model regression, (d) autoscale config, or (e) external provider.
   - Owner assignment: whoever has the shortest path to action takes lead (model-serving, infra-autoscale, region-oncall).

2) Safe action (5–15 minutes)
   - Execute reversible action from matrix. Document exact commands and timestamps in incident chat.
   - Collect evidence for hypothesis: sampling of tokens, stack traces, queue depth, autoscaler events.

3) Stabilize and measure (15–60 minutes)
   - Observe for minimum stabilization window (default 15 minutes unless otherwise specified).
   - If stable, move to controlled secondary remediation (scale, config changes).
   - If unstable or degraded continues, escalate to incident commander and consider customer-facing mitigations.

4) Post-incident remediation runway (60–120 minutes)
   - Implement durable fixes (autoscaler thresholds, caching policy changes, tenant gating).
   - Schedule a verification canary and a rollback plan for any durable change.

Evidence checklist (minimum artifacts to capture before destructive change where possible)

- Timestamped alert metrics and dashboards (P50/P95/P99).
- Sampled request records (token counts, model id, client id) for 1–3 minutes pre- and post-action.
- Node/GPU resource utilization and queue depths.
- Autoscaler events and controller logs.
- Any rollout metadata (git sha, image tag, config diff).
- Chat log with decision timestamps.

Operational tooling snippets (examples you can paste)

- Capture a 3-minute metric snapshot (prometheus query via CLI):

curl -sG "https://prometheus/api/v1/query_range" --data-urlencode "query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=\"/v1/generate\"}[1m])) by (le))" --data-urlencode "start=$(date -u -d '3 minutes ago' +%s)" --data-urlencode "end=$(date -u +%s)" --data-urlencode "step=15"

- Apply tenant soft cap (example API call to rate-limiter service):

POST /api/v1/tenant-controls/limits HTTP/1.1
Host: rate-limiter.example.internal
Content-Type: application/json

{"tenant_id":"tenant-123","qps_limit":10,"mode":"soft"}

- Emergency rollback of model variant (k8s style):

kubectl -n runtime rollout undo deployment/model-serving --to-revision=42

SLO and error budget guardrails (recommended thresholds)

- Default production SLOs:
  - Availability (5xx / total): 99.95% monthly
  - Latency: P95 < 250ms, P99 < 800ms for interactive routes
  - Embeddings endpoints: P95 < 120ms

- Error budget policies:
  - Soft alert: 10% of monthly error budget consumed in 24 hours -> notify service owner and runbook lead.
  - Actionable alert: 25% of monthly error budget consumed in 6 hours -> SRE oncall review and protective throttles considered.
  - Emergency: 50% of monthly error budget consumed in 1 hour -> open incident, immediate mitigation required.

Capacity planning anchors used by this playbook

- Provisioning headroom: Keep 30% spare GPU headroom for burst absorption per region unless contractual commitments require lower.
- Warm pools: maintain a minimum hot-model warm pool equal to 10% of average peak concurrent requests per model.
- Soft vs hard capacity lanes: define admission-control lanes for background, best-effort, and foreground customer traffic.

Runbook examples (executable sections)

1) Model hot-loop triage runbook (fast path)
   - Step 0: Owner (model-serving oncall) claims and records ETA.
   - Step 1: Query top 50 requests by tokens in last 5 minutes:
     - API: GET /internal/requests/top?window=5m&sort=tokens&limit=50
   - Step 2: If >10 requests share identical prompt prefix, enable prefix-KV caching for that route:
     - Command: POST /internal/cache/prefix/enable {"route":"/v1/generate","ttl_s":3600}
   - Step 3: If queue depth > 80% and GPU utilization > 90%: route 20% of traffic to quantized variant using traffic-split API.

2) Autoscaler stabilization runbook (fast path)
   - Step 0: Owner (infra-autoscale) record current replica count and HPA status.
   - Step 1: Patch HPA stabilization window: kubectl -n infra patch hpa/model-serve --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/behavior/scaleDown/stabilizationWindowSeconds","value":300}]'
   - Step 2: Set temporarily pinned replica count: kubectl -n infra scale deployment/model-serve --replicas=10
   - Step 3: Monitor for 20 minutes. If stable, plan adjusted HPA threshold with staging test.

Post-incident review & evidence standard

- Postmortem must include: timeline with action timestamps, hypothesis tested, evidence artifacts (metric snapshots, request samples, logs), remediation decision rationale, follow-up work (owner + ETA).
- Evidence is scored during review: S (sufficient), I (insufficient), N (not collected). Any S/I/N marked as I or N requires remediation before similar action is allowed without additional approvals.

Metrics and dashboards to include in the incident page

- Per-route latency heatmap (P50/P95/P99 by route).
- Token rate broken down by tenant and model.
- GPU queue length and warm-pool availability timeline.
- Autoscaler events and K8s pod churn.
- Error budget burn rate chart (hourly and cumulative).

Escalation and communication checklist

1. Incident commander declares mitigation and posts summary in #incidents.
2. Notify oncall roster and service owner.
3. If customer-visible degradation > 30 minutes, trigger customer notification template.

Template: "We are investigating elevated latency on [service]. We’ve applied temporary mitigations and will provide an update by [ETA]."

Governance and training

- Quarterly tabletop exercises should validate at least two matrix entries (regional failover and tenant surge) end-to-end.
- Capacity DR test annually for each region: fail one availability zone and validate failover under synthetic load.
- New SRE hires complete a remediation simulation using this playbook within their first 30 days.

Appendix: configuration examples

- Example alert rule (Prometheus-style):

ALERT SLOHighBurnRate
IF (increase(rate(slo_error_count[5m])) / increase(rate(slo_total_count[5m]))) > 0.1
FOR 5m
LABELS { severity = "page" }

- Example admission-control lanes table:

| Lane | Description | Default behavior | Max window |
| Foreground | Customer-facing interactive requests | Lowest latency, prioritized | 5s |
| Background | Batch or low-priority tasks | Throttled under pressure, queued | 300s |
| Best-effort | Non-critical telemetry or bulk jobs | Dropped when system under stress | 60s |
